Neural network · solar physics · real NREL data

It never saw a real solar panel. Then it caught a dead string the day it died.

SunDoctor learned what can go wrong with a solar array only from physics simulations: sun and clouds, dust and rain, shade from trees and rows, snow, trackers that stop turning, inverters running out of headroom, strings of panels going dark. Shown the power and temperature from one real inverter, with or without a sunlight sensor, it says what is wrong, day by day, with error bars.

Real cases

24 identical inverters in California. One answer key.

A farm in California's Sacramento Valley has 24 identical inverters, each fed by six strings of 20 panels, under the same sky. When one string dies, that inverter drops to five sixths of its siblings. SunDoctor never sees the siblings. It reads one inverter at a time, as it would read a home system, and the other 23 grade its answers.

New in v2 · No sensor needed

Most home systems don't measure sunlight. Now it doesn't have to.

A farm has an irradiance sensor; a rooftop usually has only what the inverter app shows: power, every few minutes. Version 2 was trained on half its fortnights with the sensor taken away, so it learns what a clear sky should give from the sun's position alone, and reads the clouds from the shape of the day. Below, the same string failure, read twice.

What power-only mode sees

Inverter 11's output divided by what a cloudless sky would give at that moment. Clouds and faults both show as red; the network has to tell them apart.

How much the sensor is worth

The same exams as with a sensor, on the same California farm, with the sensor's data thrown away. Version 1 was never trained this way.

A home system usually reports power per inverter or per panel, at 5 to 15 minutes. SunDoctor needs the array's tilt, direction and size, and air temperature from any weather service.

New in v2 · A second farm

Colorado: trackers, snow, and a sensor that read half the sunlight for three years.

NREL's system 9068 is a 4.7 MW plant near Kersey, Colorado: two inverters, eight power modules, 224 single-axis trackers that turn the panels to follow the sun. It sees snow every winter. Its answer keys come from its own instruments: every tracker's angle against where physics says it should point, the eight modules against each other, and the irradiance sensors against output on cold days. Its main sensor read about half the true sunlight from May 2019 to October 2022, so with-sensor results use only the days it worked; power-only mode uses all of them.

The Colorado exam, every module-day for six years

No Colorado data was used in training or in choosing between rungs, though rung 8's weather change was prompted by rung 6's snow misses here (see the limits). "Flagged" uses fixed thresholds; AUC is how well the daily estimate ranks real events above everything else (0.5 is a coin toss, 1 is perfect).

Break it yourself

Pick a fortnight. Add a fault. Watch the diagnosis.

These are three real, healthy fortnights of one inverter. Every slider adds a fault with physics: a dead string switches off one sixth of the array, dust dims it, a tree blocks the low sun, a smaller inverter clips the peak, a snowstorm buries the panels until the snow slides off. The network then runs here in your browser and diagnoses what you did, without being told. Switch to power only to see how it does without the sunlight sensor.

The exam

California, graded three ways, on data it never trained on.

First, the 23 siblings grade every inverter-day. Second, known faults are added to real healthy fortnights, so the true answer is known exactly but the weather, sensors and noise are real. Third, its long-run view is compared with RdTools, NREL's standard analysis library.

How it works

Physics in, diagnosis out.

The simulator

Every training example is a made-up system somewhere between 20° and 52° north, fixed at any tilt and direction or on single-axis trackers, under a fortnight of generated weather. The sun is placed exactly, clouds come and go, the panels heat up, and the inverter runs out of headroom. Then things go wrong: strings die and get fixed, dust builds until rain washes it, trees and rows cast shadows, snow falls and slides off, trackers stick or stow, inverters trip. Two in five lose their sunlight sensor.

The carpet plot

Solar engineers call a picture of days down and time of day across a carpet plot. SunDoctor reads one as an image. Every system is lined up on solar time, so noon is always the middle column. A dead string is a horizontal step. Shading is a notch that drifts with the seasons. Clipping is a flat lid. Dust is a slow fade that rain resets.

P(t) = min( PAC,max, ηinv · PDC0 · Geff/1000 · [1 + γ(Tcell − 25 °C)] · fonline · (1 − s) )

The network

A 2-D convolutional network reads twelve channels per pixel: power, measured sunlight (or a flag saying there is none), clear-sky sunlight, two physics expectations, temperature, sun angles, a data mask and the system's own healthy level. Dilated convolutions then compare days. Every output comes with its own error bar.

Use it

One Python file, one weights file, any CSV.

Give it a CSV of AC power and air temperature, with plane-of-array irradiance if you have it, plus where the array is and how it faces or tracks. You get a day-by-day diagnosis and the kilowatt-hours lost to each cause. It needs only numpy, and pandas to read the CSV.
